parts.text:
1
What must be included in a record of a physical quantity?
A
an integer value for the quantity
B
an SI unit
C
a numerical value for the quantity
D
a unit expressed in base units

hints: Focus on the word must in the question - which requirement applies to every record of a physical quantity without exception?
Recall that a physical quantity is written as magnitude times unit, for example $l = 2.5 \text{ cm}$.
Test each option for a counterexample: can a length be $2.5$ rather than an integer, and can it use $\text{cm}$ rather than $\text{m}$ or base units?
walkthrough: Identify the definition: a measurement of a physical quantity has the form $\text{quantity} = \text{numerical value} \times \text{unit}$, for example $m = 1.20 \text{ kg}$.
This means two parts are needed to make the record meaningful: how much there is and what scale it is measured on.
The numerical value does not have to be an integer - values like $2.5$ or $0.34$ are common, so an integer is not a must.
The unit does not have to be the SI unit and does not have to be expanded into base units - $\text{cm}$, $\text{km h}^{-1}$ and $\text{kW}$ are all acceptable units.
Therefore the only feature that must always be present is a numerical value for the quantity. This is option C.

A.explanation: A value can be a decimal, fraction or with uncertainty, so it does not have to be an integer such as $2$ or $5$.

B.explanation: A valid unit such as $\text{cm}$ or $\text{eV}$ is acceptable, so it does not have to be the SI unit such as $\text{m}$ or $\text{J}$.

C.explanation: A physical quantity is defined as a numerical magnitude times a unit, so the numerical value must always be recorded.

D.explanation: Derived units such as $\text{N}$ or $\text{V}$ are acceptable, so there is no requirement to write the unit only in base units such as $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$.
